name: PlayerDeploymentAreaTableHasSevenHundredSixtyEightRows
summary: The origin of the player's deployment grid comes from a 12-byte-row table of 768 rows in the executable (row number in the u16 at +10), indexed by the deployment area ids in variables 53 and 54 with no bound check; the EntryArea data table adds the slot list of the same id.

behavior.text: the table starts at 0x1407AE2D0; the u16 at +10 of every row equals its own row number, 0..767.

the area id read from variable 53 + i (i below variable 52) is multiplied by 12 with no comparison with the table size; bytes +4 and +5 are the origin tile, +6 the height layer, +7 packs an orientation and a size nibble.
the EntryArea rows of the same id (key2 = slot, up to 25 read) give one byte per slot; a 5 x 5 grid of slots is built around the origin and oriented by +7.
stock area ids lie in 256..722; random battles use 513..569.

notes: The table is not in the table census yet.
open_questions: ? the meaning of the first dword of a row and of bytes +8 and +9.

name: PoisonAndRegenActAtTheEndOfTheUnitsTurn
summary: Poison and Regen change HP when the turn of the unit ends: Battle_TurnEngine phase 19 writes max HP / 8 as damage (Poison) or as a heal (Regen, only when not poisoned) into the result block of the unit, which the game then applies as an action result. A unit that is Crystal, KO, Jumping, Stone or Chest is skipped.

behavior.text: after the units of the turn are finished the engine goes to phase 19; for the active unit it resets the result block, then +0x64 bit 0x80 (Poison) writes max HP >> 3 at +6 and 0x80 at +0x27, else bit 0x40 (Regen) writes max HP >> 3 at +8 and 0x40; a non-zero +0x27 returns the unit with 0x300 so the result is applied.
the text of the game for Poison (UIStatusEffect 25) says the damage comes at the end of the turn of the unit.
with max HP below 8 the change is 0 (the shift floors).

open_questions: ? live: the order of the Poison damage and the Invisibility / terrain steps (phases 15, 17) in one turn end.

name: PoolRecordKeepsItsSpriteAcrossTheReset
summary: A look pool record keeps the sprite it holds (byte +1) after LookPool_ResetForBattleLoad, and the load pass skips the classic file of a queued sprite that any record's +1 already names; only the battle setup clears +1 of every record.

behavior.text: LookPool_ResetForBattleLoad sets byte +0 of each record to 0 and leaves +1 and the data.
CharaPalette_ReloadForShape's pass 2 compares the queue word with byte +1 of all 15 records (claimed or not) and, on a hit, skips the classic file read for that entry.
LookPool_ClaimForSprite returns the first record whose +1 equals the sprite before it looks for a free one, so a reset record is reused for the same sprite.
the battle setup sub_140210AF0 sets +1 of all 15 records to 0 (0x140210BF9) before the resume restore.
so in stock a sprite number always names the same files, and a reused record's data stay valid.

name: PortraitCodeIsAByteOnTheSaveRecordPath
summary: On the save-record path a portrait code can only carry 256 distinct faces: the code reader refuses a code with bit 8 or 9 and the cell function returns the low byte.

behavior.text: sub_14032AB3C returns -1 for (code & 0x300) != 0; PortraitCode_FillCell returns (uint8_t)code and puts bits 10 and 11 into the colour.
mode word 0 or 2: no code gives -1, 146 codes map (largest face 204), 110 come back as themselves (50 of them 206..255); mode words 1 and 5: the 50 codes 206..255 give -1.
codes above 255 (only if one arrived): mode word 0 returns them raw (256 .. 1299), mode word 1 gives -1.

name: PreviewBuildersReadPartyRecordCopies
summary: The unit detail and summary builders (sub_1402C185C, sub_1402C1628) read a party record copied in three parts (header from +34, middle from +48, block from +112); the header names the save slot (header + 10 = +44), and the Fitting screen's stack copy of party record 54 is such a copy.

behavior.text: the header's +10 is the save slot: sub_1402C1628 indexes the save records by it; every writer of the shared header buffer copies the party record's +0x22 / +0x2A / +0x2E.

open_questions: ? sub_1403783F0 writes a header of its own (its +10 may be stale).

name: PseudoEffectWordIsASixteenBitEventOperand
summary: An effect word of 512 or more selects a row of the 37-word pseudo effect table (row = word - 512, row 0 when 37 or more) and the effect number is masked to 9 bits; event command class 0x18 sets the word, which the event state keeps as a 16-bit value with -1 meaning none.

behavior.text: Effect_SelectForAbility compares the effect word with 512 as a SIGNED int; for a word of 512 or more it tests word - 512 below 0x25 (an immediate byte, so at most 127 could ever be encoded there) and takes that row, else row 0; words below 512 use the ability effect number table (bound 0x1C6, else row 0). A negative word (0x8000..0xFFFE as a 16-bit value) takes the ability branch and row 0, never the pseudo table.

the class 0x18 case of EventScript_Run builds its operand as a 16-bit little-endian word from the script bytes 1 and 2 and stores it as a word at 0x140D40930; the event state snapshot copies it as a 16-bit value at +554; the effect starter (sub_14023A0B4) reads it with a sign extension, treats -1 as none and otherwise passes it as an int to EventEffect_Start, which calls Effect_SelectForAbility.

so the highest word that reaches the pseudo table from an event script is 32,767, which is row 32,255; BattleAct_SetupEffect also passes the action's ability number as the effect word (a stock ability number is below 512).
the number read from the row is a 16-bit value: a negative one (bit 15) means no effect, and the number is masked with 0x1FF (nine bits) after that test, so bits 9..14 are ignored.

notes: Two other callers pass constants below 512.
open_questions: ? which stock scripts use the command, and whether any word above 548 occurs in them.

name: QuitLoopExit
scope: how the quit request ends the main loop
summary: Game_Main runs App_RunFrame in a loop and leaves it when it returns 0; App_RunFrame returns whether the quit request byte is 0.

behavior.text: Game_Main (0x14002BD50) tests App_RunFrame's result right after the call (0x14002BE57) and leaves the loop on 0; App_RunFrame returns whether byte +0x5F0 of the application object is 0 (the compare at 0x14002A872). So the quit request `g_Application` +0x5F0 = 1 ends the loop after the current frame.

name: QuitRequest
scope: how the game ends itself or hands over to the Classic executable
summary: The quit request byte of the application object and every path that sets it.

behavior.text: `g_Application` (0x140C6AD30) +1520 (byte) is the quit request. Set to 1 by `App_LaunchClassic` (after starting the Classic exe), by `UILauncher_Update` when its exit fade ends, by `UIAgentFFTOSystem_StateExitGame` (a dialog's answer, event 2), and by `App_RunFrame` (0x14002A442) when `IsDebuggerPresent()` is true or `Debug_DetectCaptureTools` reports a capture tool.
the main loop ends on it (every exit path writes it; the reader was not traced).

name: RandomBattleModeSelectsTheLightingVariantOfAMapsTextures
summary: A battle started from a random encounter runs MapRow_SelectVariation in its 'random battle' branch, which always yields a kind code from 1 to 6, and the name builder then reads the second name array of each texture row at index kind - 1. Only the maps of the random-encounter set (71..90 except 73) carry names there (the lighting variants _ra to _rf); every other map has an empty second array, so such a map requests no map texture and no system texture in that mode and draws as a black void with the deployment tiles floating. The same map draws normally when the mode global reads 0 at load.

behavior.text: MapRow_SelectVariation reads the 32-bit global at 0x141853C08 first. Not 1: it matches the map row's variation structs by scene variables and writes kind code 0, and the textures come from the first name array at the variation index. 1: kind code from scene variable 35 (v35) and 36 (v36): v35 = 0 or 5 and above: 4 if v36 is non-zero else 1; v35 = 1 or 2: 5 if v36 non-zero else 2; v35 = 3 or 4: 6 if v36 non-zero else 3; the variation index is the last struct whose field at +16 equals the kind code, else 0.

the global read 0 on the world map and 1 once the battle of a random encounter was loading (title card, deployment); scene variables read 35 = 0, 36 = 1, 48 = 0, 39 = 0 and the name builder was called with kind 4 (index 3); another battle read kind 1 (index 0) and another kind 2 (index 1) for stock map 84, whose requested files were the _rb set (lut_chara_a_0_rb.tga, gt_0_map084_map_lighting_rb.tga).

the keys of RefinedBgTexture rows whose second name array is not empty are exactly 71, 72, 74..90; the other 99 keys (maps 0..70, 73, 91..116) have empty second arrays. These are the maps 71..90 the random-encounter table names (byte 22 values 71, 72, 74..90).

stock maps 10 and 20 (anim file, rows present, texture folders present) in that mode: the mesh loaded (result 0), the texture gate was open, the name builder ran with kind 4 or 1 and returned no name, and no texture file of the map was requested (no gt_ and no lut_chara file); the deployment view was a black void. Stock maps 72, 84 and 85 in that mode drew their terrain.

with the global written to 0 before the map load task ran, stock map 10 requested bg/textures/010/lut_chara_a_0.tga and the rest of its first-array files and drew its stone-dungeon terrain; map 20 likewise (MapAnim_Load and MapAnim_ReadRows were entered and the anim file was requested). Map 72 with an anim file drew in mode 1 without any change, so an anim file is not what blanks a map.

a battle started from a story event leaves the global at a value other than 1, which is why the story maps draw there; a story battle was not read for it (?). What the global means for the rest of the battle was not studied; only the picture at deployment was seen with it at 0.

notes: Scene variables 35 and 36 change from battle to battle (kind 1, 2 and 4 were all seen on the same world-map spot), so the lighting variant of a random battle is not fixed by the map.

name: RandomEncounterRowByte22IsTheBattleMapId
summary: A random battle at a battleground takes its battle map from byte 22 of the encounter row, not from a scenario setup record: the row's byte 22 becomes variable 51 when the world-map screen ends, the chosen formation byte becomes variable 50, 0x200 plus the row's battle number becomes variable 53, variable 52 is 1 and variable 39 is 0.

behavior.text: only locations 24..42 have rows (three per location); the row is the one whose first byte equals the arrival road.
byte 22 holds 85 for Mandalia Plain, 74 for the Siedge Weald, 83 for Zeirchele Falls and so on; for all 19 locations the place name of that map equals the location's name.

WorldEncounter_Roll stores the picked formation byte, byte 22 and 0x200 + byte 1 in three globals; sub_140248254 writes the formation to variable 50, 1 to variable 52, the battle number to variable 53 and 0 to variable 39, and keeps byte 22 for the exit of the world-map screen task, which writes it to variable 51.
the same roll serves the walk onto a battleground and the 'Search for Enemies' action (forced roll).
variable 39 is 0, so the scenario setup applier finds no record and leaves variable 51 as the world-map screen wrote it.

notes: The field was not decoded before; the byte is an unsigned value 0..255.
open_questions: ? whether anything between the screen's exit and the scene entry rewrites variable 51.

name: RasterizerSnapsTo1_256Px
scope: GPU (the test machine's GPU and driver)
summary: Vertex positions are snapped to 1/256 of a pixel (rounded to nearest) before rasterization, so a UI quad at a third of a pixel (the 2/3 screen scale) is drawn from slightly moved corners and samples its texture at slightly moved positions.

behavior.basis: (back-buffer captures 2026-10-30, the finger cursor's glove at 12 frozen phases, background captured with the glove hidden)
behavior.text: redoing the glove's draw with corners rounded to 1/256 px and 1/256 texel weights reproduces 99.4 % of the glove's 10076 changed values exactly (max 1); exact corners give 93.3 %, truncated corners 84.7 %, a 1/16 px grid 65.4 %.
D3D requires at least 8 bits of sub-pixel precision; this GPU uses exactly that, rounded.

name: ResumedBattleRestoresUnitRecordsWithoutUnpack
scope: resuming a battle from an autosave: where the live unit records come from
summary: A battle resumed from an autosave gets its live unit records (g_UnitSaveData) from the battle snapshot region through Battle_RestoreSceneVars, and SaveWork_UnpackToLive does not run for it: the resume entry unpacks only when the payload part count is 0, and otherwise only sets a flag.

behavior.text: Battle_SnapshotLiveState(work, direction) moves the live state between the live globals and the work block with two memmoves of 0x7E90 bytes between g_UnitSaveData and the work base: direction 0 copies live to work (capture), direction 1 copies work to live (restore); the item stores follow in the same call.
it is called by Battle_SaveCapture (capture) and by Battle_RestoreSceneVars (with the snapshot buffer at 0x14089BC68 and direction 1).

Battle_RestoreSceneVars (0x1402CE5C8) is called from sub_140210AF0 at 0x140210C51; it restores seven scene variables, then the live unit records and item stores through Battle_SnapshotLiveState, the 21 battle units, the look queue and the look pool.

Save_ResumeCheckpoint (0x1402D03D8) reads the payload part count (clamped to 2; a missing object counts as 2). Only when it is 0 does it copy the checkpoint copy into the work copy and tail-jump to SaveWork_UnpackToLive; otherwise it only sets dword_142E7FF68 = 1 (also when the header import fails).

a battle autosave carries a battle snapshot (part count not 0), so a resumed battle takes the flag-only path: its live unit records come from the snapshot copy, and SaveWork_UnpackToLive does not run for it.
SaveWork_UnpackToLive did not run during a cold battle resume, while a world-map autosave load ran it.

notes: Evidence: IDA decompiles of Battle_SnapshotLiveState, Battle_RestoreSceneVars, Save_ResumeCheckpoint read in full on 2026-11-09; the live observation was made on 2026-11-09.
open_questions: ? what dword_142E7FF68 = 1 starts for the battle path; ? where the part count is set by the writer.

name: ResumeLoadsTheLookStateTwice
summary: A battle resumed from a payload copies the payload twice around the scene-variable restore, builds no scene unit but restores the scene-unit records whole, and rebuilds existing scene units from the restored slot and pool indices.

behavior.text: sub_140210AF0, load mode 1 (0x142FF9E2C == 1): 0x140210C4C sub_140257354 (-> sub_1402181EC), 0x140210C51 Battle_RestoreSceneVars, then 0x140210CFF sub_140257354 again and 0x140210D04 Battle_RestoreCapture: the resume payload is copied twice, the second time after the scene variables, the queue and the look pool are restored.

sub_1402181EC with a battle payload (kind 1) copies 668,112 bytes into g_SaveBattleSnapshot (0x1408167A0; the region holds g_UnitLookPoolIndex 0x140822D58) and 16 dwords into g_HdSheetEntryBySlot[13..28] (0x142E7FEA0 .. 0x142E7FEE0) from the payload's header (+276), then inflates the payload's image page with PackEntry_Inflate.

Battle_RestoreCapture copies the battle unit table (0x2A00 bytes from 0x140898134), the party records and the pool face values (sub_140304BEC mode 1 from 0x1408B88F0); it does not touch the look queue or g_LookPool.

a resumed battle builds no scene unit: the scene load state dword_140D3A86C comes back with the capture, and Battle_RestoreCapture calls SceneUnits_SaveRestore(capture, 1), which copies the 16 scene-unit records back (0x140D30030, 0x5480 bytes), recomputes their frame / sequence table pointers (+0x220 / +0x228 and the saved copies +0x230 / +0x238) from each record's sprite byte, rebuilds the scene list from the in-use flags, links each battle unit through g_UnitSceneSlotIndex (scene +0x148 = unit) and restores g_ClutImage (0x1C00 bytes) and g_ClutManager (0x86DC bytes).

SceneUnit_BuildFromQueueEntry in load mode 1 rebuilds a unit's existing scene unit (slot from g_UnitSceneSlotIndex[unit +444], none -> no build; the record is not linked again when it was in use; pool record from g_UnitLookPoolIndex); in mode 0 it takes the scene slot named by its slot argument and links it.

sub_14026E838 in load mode 1 skips the classic VRAM frame uploads of pools 0..8; the palette copy into the record (+0x30D6, 512 bytes, then CharShape_ApplyClut), the face value and the record data copy (+2, 12,500 bytes from file +0x9000) run in every mode.

a resumed battle restores the 15 look pool records whole (0x2FA8A bytes: claim, sprite, palette at +0x30D6, data) and g_UnitLookPoolIndex for every battle unit, benched ones (no scene unit) included; seen live 2026-11-13: benched goblins kept record 0 naming their shape while the field goblins used record 1.

open_questions: ? how g_UnitSceneSlotIndex gets its entries back between the two payload copies is covered by SceneUnits_SaveRestore (I); the queue entries' unit pointers across a process restart were not read.

name: RumourNewFlagsAreIndexedByTheLowByteOfTheId
summary: Every reader and the writer of the rumour new flags guards the index with a test of the LOW BYTE of the id (taken as a signed byte, it must be 0..63, and that byte is the index), so an id whose low byte is 0..63 indexes the 64 pairs whatever its upper bits are.

behavior.text: four places address the pairs: the builder's read (0x14036EED3), two reads in Tavern_HasNewEntries (0x140345270, 0x1403453FA), the clear in TavernMenu_OnCommand (0x14019D76A, through the base 0x1411A7280 + 0x19); and the reset loop of sub_14033FB84 (64 pairs set to {1, 1}).
the save stores the pairs by its field schema from the fixed block at 0x1411A7280 (bar.uwasa.menu_new[64] at +25), not through these instructions.
moving the cursor onto a rumour in the list clears its new flag.

name: RuntimeJobListCanLiveInAnyBlockWithinReach
summary: Every reference to g_RuntimeJobList is a 32-bit displacement (four rip-relative `lea`, six reads through the image base plus a sign-extended index), the list is in the zero-filled tail of the data section and no data pointer names it, so it can be moved to a larger block by rewriting ten displacements.

behavior.basis: (census of every instruction of the code section, base relocation directory)
behavior.text: the ten code references are the only references to the 96 bytes of the list; none is a data pointer, so the base relocation directory needs no change.
the list lies past the raw data of the section that holds it (the bss tail): it is zero when the game starts and the game itself fills it each time JobTree_FillJobRecords runs.

the four rip-relative `lea` (0x140367F15 in JobList_IsSelectedEntryUnflagged; 0x1403684B8, 0x1403687A5, 0x14036885A in JobTree_FillJobRecords) reach any block within 2 GB of the instruction; the six reads in JobScreen_UpdateState add a 32-bit displacement to the image base held in rsi, so the block must also lie within 2 GB above or below the image base.

in JobScreen_UpdateState the reads at 0x140368D06 and 0x140368D42 index the list with g_JobListSelectedEntry (sign-extended from 16 bits); the reads at 0x140368DB9, 0x140368E7D, 0x140368EC5 and 0x140368F9A index it with the result of the cursor call just before (sign-extended from 16 or 32 bits); so the reads accept an index up to 32767, the range of the int16 length.

the reads at 0x140368D06, 0x140368D42, 0x140368DB9, 0x140368E7D and 0x140368EC5 load a 16-bit entry; 0x140368F9A loads only its low byte; JobTree_FillJobRecords tests the 0x2000 and 0x4000 flags with word tests through the register of its `lea` at 0x14036885A (second test at 0x140368884).

behavior.basis: (offline test on a copy of the exe mapped into a test process, with the ten displacements rewritten)
behavior.text: JobList_IsSelectedEntryUnflagged, called natively, reads entry 1000 and entry 1279 of the 1280-word block and its 0x4000 flag; the 48 stock words stay zero (never read or written).
the game writes at most 23 words into the list and reads only those.

open_questions: ? not run in the game yet: a Change Job list of more than 48 entries (scrolling to the end, selecting and changing to a late entry, the preview of a late entry); ? the time the fill loop takes over about 1000 positions when the window scrolls.

name: RuntimeJobListIs48WordsFollowedByAnotherGlobal
summary: g_RuntimeJobList is 96 bytes (48 words) and the next object in memory is g_UIChosenItemId, so the list cannot grow in place; the length is a signed 16-bit word kept at another address.

behavior.text: g_RuntimeJobList is at 0x143C51890; g_UIChosenItemId is at 0x143C518F0 (list + 0x60) and is read by sub_14036AC38 and written by sub_14036AC74; g_JobListSelectedEntry (int16) is at 0x143C51880, 16 bytes before the list.

the length g_RuntimeJobListLen is a separate int16 at 0x143C510D8; it is written by JobTree_FillJobRecords (two stores, the second sets 1 for a unit hidden from the tree), read by JobList_IsSelectedEntryUnflagged (compare with 2) and by the fill loop (signed 16-bit compare and conditional move).

the list has 10 code references, none outside three functions: JobList_IsSelectedEntryUnflagged (1 lea), JobTree_FillJobRecords (3 lea: 0x1403684B8 passes it to the builder, 0x1403687A5 reads an entry, 0x14036885A tests flags), JobScreen_UpdateState (6 reads through image base + rva + index*2, at 0x140368D06, 0x140368D42, 0x140368DB9, 0x140368E7D, 0x140368EC5, 0x140368F9A).
the stock builder writes at most 22 entries and the 0xFFFF terminator (23 words).

name: SaveCardJobIsTheLeadersPartyJobWordLowByte
summary: The slot card's job byte (slot image +274) is the low byte of the leader's 16-bit party job word: SaveWork_PackFromParty picks the first party unit whose marker (+114) is 1..3 and passes its word +36 to SaveWork_PackFromLive, which stores its low byte (0x140218F9D). Only the Classic title reads it back; the Enhanced save list does not show a job.

behavior.text: SaveWork_PackFromParty: leader = first g_PartyUnits[i] with (byte +114) - 1 <= 2; clears the hero name (+257, 16 bytes), +273 = 0xFE, then SaveWork_PackFromLive(slot, word +36, word +0, index).
SaveWork_PackFromLive stores its job argument's low byte at +274 and the next argument's at +275 (0x140218F9D / 0x140218FA3).
with a leader whose party job word read 0x1F4 (500), a manual save held 244 at +274.

the reads of +274: SaveSlot_BuildClassicTitle (movzx at 0x14021C17D); SaveLoadList_FillItem (the Enhanced list) fills level, location, next event, date, play time, clear marks and sprite records, no job.

name: ScenarioSetupRecordFeedsTheBattleSceneVariables
scope: engine (scene entry of an event or battle)
summary: When a scene starts, the routine that applies the scenario setup record finds the record of the current event number (scene variable 39) in the 24-byte table of 887 records and writes the scene variables the battle load reads: the battle map id (variable 51) from a signed byte at +2, the entry key (50), up to two deployment area ids (53, 54) and their count (52).

behavior.text: the search is linear over at most 887 records and ends at the first record whose event number (u16 at +0) is 0; 713 stock records are used (event numbers 1..743) and 174 are free.
the map id is the signed byte at +2; the byte at +3 is a separate field (high nibble to variable 48, low nibble to variable 35), so the two bytes are not one 16-bit map word.

SceneVar_Write stores a negative value reduced to its low byte, so a map byte of 128..255 reaches variable 51 as 128..255; variable 51 is a 32-bit cell and the scene entry copies it into the 32-bit battle map id.

the u16 at +7 is the entry key (variable 50) and is written only when it is not 0; the u16 at +9 and +11 are deployment area ids (variables 53 and 54), variable 52 counts the non-zero ones, and the signed byte at +17 goes to variable 511 only when the one at +9 is not 0.

the u16 at +22 is a key of the table EnhancedBattleEvent; the routine returns before writing variable 51 when that key has no row, when the key has 16 or more entries, or when the collected list reaches 512 words.
Scenario_CheckBattleRecord continues a battle only for a record whose byte +20 is exactly 0x80 (144 stock records); 65 records hold 0x81 and 20 hold 0x82.
the per-event words built from bytes +18..+20 fill an array of 887 words indexed by event number, which the battle capture copies whole (0x6EE bytes): event numbers stay below 887.

notes: Event 93 keeps the current value of variable 51 instead of the record's map byte. In the resume case (scene mode 1) the routine reads the record of the saved event number.
open_questions: ? the meaning of byte +20 values 0x81 and 0x82; ? bytes +5, +6, +13, +14 and +15..+16; ? whether the 59 stock records whose key at +22 has no EnhancedBattleEvent row are ever started.

name: ScenarioWordLinksRecordsByATenBitKeyAndLivesInTheBattleCapture
summary: The scenario setup records are turned into one 16-bit word per EVENT NUMBER (an 887-word array indexed by scene variable 39); a word holds a 10-bit link to another record by event number plus flag bits, and the battle capture and restore copy the 887 words at a fixed place.

behavior.text: the builder walks the records until the first one whose event number is 0 (or 887 records) and stores, for each, the word byte +18 + (byte +19 << 10), OR byte +20 << 8 (16 bits), at the index given by the record's OWN event number, not its row.

the mid-event refresh finds the linked record by the key (word and 0xFF) plus ((word shifted right 2) and 0x300): the link has 10 bits, 0 to 1,023; bits 8, 9 and 12 to 15 are flags, tested together with the mask 0xF300 by three battle functions and by the event runner, and the word is also tested for sign and for zero.

sixteen instructions address the array (census of the whole image): ten index it by an event number (scene variable 39 or the message index global) with no bound, two are the capture copies, six write words 400..404 directly after the builder loop (401 = 0, 402 = 8000h, 403 = 0, 400 and 404 = 8000h or 8200h by scene variable 510).

the battle capture and the restore copy the 0x6EE bytes (887 words) into the capture block at 0x14081CCF2, directly after the 0x2800-byte event script buffer and directly before the next captured byte at 0x14081D3E0.

the row bound 0x377 is an immediate in three places: the battle record check (cmp), and two loads into a register in ScenarioSetup_ApplyRecord, the second of which bounds both the word builder and the record search after it.
the event number is read as byte0 | (int16)(byte1 << 8), sign-extended: a number of 32,768 or more never matches var 39 and would index the word array negatively.

notes: The row count and the word array length are the same constant, but they bound different things: rows (the loop bounds) and event numbers (the array index).
open_questions: ? whether any save slot (as opposed to the battle capture) carries the array.

name: SceneSkipState
scope: every skippable story scene: event scripts (world map, town, battle) and movies
summary: Whether the scene on screen can be skipped with the pause overlay + hold, and which kind of scene it is, read from memory without any input.

behavior.text: only two objects consume the hold action 0x5D (Input_TestAction / sub_1400F144C / sub_1400F1510 / sub_1400F0E98 with 0x5D): EventControl (EventControl_PausedTick, EventControl_TryOpenPause) and MovieControl (MovieControl_PausedTick, MovieControl_TryOpenPause). Any scene the overlay can skip is an event script or a movie.

event script: running = low dword of g_EventScriptActive (u32 0x142FF9EC0) == 1. Skippable = EventSkip_IsAvailable: viewer case (event variable 508 != 0, variable 39 not in 410..425, u32 0x141849E10 == 0) or u32 0x142E7FB3C != 0 and u32 0x142FF9E54 == 0 and u32 0x142FF9E50 != 0 and u32 0x142FF9E0C == 0 and u32 0x142FF9EBC != 2. All inputs are plain globals set before the overlay exists; opening the overlay writes none of them.

the event's armed flag (u32 0x142FF9E50) is decided when EventScript_LoadCurrent loads an event whose number (variable 39) differs from the last loaded one (s32 0x140782A94): 1 when EventId (NXD 156) byte +32 is set, when the event is one of 517, 530, 549, 551, 524, 553, 569, 579, or in the viewer case; otherwise 0. EventScript_Run clears it when the script ends.

skip-once: EventScript_Run sets u32 0x142FF9EBC to 1 at its start for events with EventId byte +36 (117, 170, 179, 213, 222, 298, 374, 427, 483, 489), for battles whose NXD 96 row has byte +147/+148/+149 set, and for events 524, 530, 569; else 0. Taking a skip turns 1 into 2, after which EventSkip_IsAvailable is false for the rest of that script.

an event script that runs again under the same event number (LoadCurrent sees no change) is not re-armed: armed was cleared at the previous script end, so it reads 0 and the scene is not skippable. Battle message events started by BattleMsg_Dispatch go through the same EventScript_TaskMain path and follow this rule.

event pause gate: EventControl_Update runs only while 0x142FF9EC0 != 0, g_ShopModeGate (0x1407D453C, enhanced flag) != 0 and u32 at qword_143CD9DD0 + 92 == 0; the overlay opens only while EventControl bytes +0x31, +0x34, +0x39 are 0. These say whether the overlay can open now, not whether the scene is skippable.

movie: g_MovieControl (u64 0x143CDA078) non-null after Movie_Start. Skippable = u8 at g_MovieControl + 0x19, rewritten every frame from movie flag 0x10 (u32 at u64(0x143CD9DC8) + 0xC8 + 0x18). Readable without input; the overlay only reads it.

MovieData (NXD 65) rows 5, 6, 7 and 9..15 (movie/enhanced/19, 10, 08, 01..07.usm) have bytes +36 and +37 set (pausable and skippable); rows 1..4 (09_ja, 20, 22, 21_ja) and 16..22 have byte +38 set and +37 clear (not skippable).
the requested / playing movie id is s32 0x142E7FB04 (-1 none): Boot_UpdateVideo starts that MovieData row.

the overlay's button guide is UIButtonGuide 502 (Resume + Skip); both overlays pass mask -3 instead of -1 when the scene is not skippable (I: bit 1 = the Skip entry), so an overlay that shows only Resume is the same answer as the passive read.

which kind each on-screen scene is (prologue narration, Orbonne chapel): the narration is not an event script loaded by number (event number reads -1 there, live 2026-10-30), so by the exhaustion above it is a movie (I), unproven live.

notes: Debugger reads (dbg.py _event_info): 'allowed' = low dword of 0x142FF9E4C is the viewer flag, 0 in normal play by design; 'armed' = 0x142FF9E50 is the real per-event flag; 'veto' = 0x142FF9E54 is 1 only while a battle scene is built; 'state' = 0x142FF9E0C is the skip state (0 none, 1 requested, 2 skipping). Detail and evidence: the function sheets named on this page.
open_questions: ? Live: armed / skip-once / event number during the Orbonne chapel scene and a world-map event; g_MovieControl + 0x19 during the prologue narration; whether mid-battle balloons reuse the battle's event number.

name: SceneUnitShapeIsTheQueueWord
summary: A scene unit's shape (sprite byte +0xA) is the sprite word of its load queue entry; a battle unit's shape byte +0x18F is written only by the unit builders and comes back in the battle snapshot, while the save keeps no shape byte.

behavior.text: SceneUnit_BuildFromQueueEntry writes the scene unit's sprite byte +0xA from its sprite argument (bpl, 0x14026EDA0) and the pool index +9; its caller CharaPalette_ReloadForShape (load step 2) passes the queue entry's word +6 as that argument.

Battle_BuildRosterTeam queues a placed unit with LookQueue_Add(unit +0x4F, +0x50, +0x51 >> 7, +0x51 & 0xF, shape, palette, 255, unit, 0) after Unit_ResolvePreviewShape (shape -> unit +0x18F, palette -> +0x190). The queue entry: bytes +0 / +1 / +2 = x, y, layer, word +4 facing, +6 sprite, +8 palette, +0xA slot, qword +0x10 unit, dword +0x18 flag; the loader passes them to SceneUnit_BuildFromQueueEntry in that order. M: the runtime test that ran LookQueue_Add on the mapped executable agreed.

the battle unit record's shape +0x18F is written only by the unit builders through Unit_ResolvePreviewShape (marker + job rule) and comes back in the battle snapshot together with the unit table, the queue words +6, the 15 look pool records (+0 claim, +1 sprite) and g_UnitLookPoolIndex.

the save's unit record (600 bytes) holds no shape byte: the menus and every fresh battle load derive the shape from the marker and the job byte (Unit_ResolvePreviewShape, from record bytes +0 and +2); the save slot summary stores up to four shapes, but only of Ramza and the guests 50..53, whose shape is their marker (job-independent). So only the battle snapshot keeps job-derived shape bytes.

scene object +0x148 points at the battle unit record (g_PreviewUnitTable entry), +0xA is the sprite byte, +0x1E a byte the formation scales by 12, +0x15C bit 2 selects the formation's +0x2F test. SceneObject_FindByUnitIndex walks `g_SceneObjectList` for the object whose record has the given unit index (+444).

name: ScreenMusicComesFromBGMTransitionRows
summary: Screens such as the title's play-mode page, the save and load list and the tavern start their music through sub_1401D9174 with a BGMTransition row number: the row names a SoundEnhanced row, whose Unknown10 is the music id bound to slot 1 and loaded.

behavior.text: opening the save and load list from the main menu ran BGMTransition row 8 (SoundEnhanced row 190, music id 41): id 41 was bound to slot 1 and track 40 was loaded.
with SoundEnhanced row 190's Unknown10 changed to 300, the same screen bound id 300 and loaded track 299 (music_00299.sab).
the world map's music on a load (id 27, slot 1) does not come from SoundEnhanced row 176 (also 27): changing that row left it unchanged.

notes: Seen 2026-11-16 on the Steam PC build.
open_questions: ? where the world map takes its music id from.

name: SecondarySkillsetListsTakeEveryUnlockedJob
summary: Both secondary-skillset collectors build the unit's job list into a 24-word stack buffer, and write into lists that hold 145 entries: the three lists the game builds them into (g_MenuList, g_JobAbilityPairList, JobScreen_FindJobOfSkillset's frame list).

behavior.text: Unit_CollectJobSkillsets and Unit_CollectJobSkillsetPairs call JobList_BuildForPartyUnit(unit, list, 1) with a 24-word list in their own frame and walk it to the 0xFFFF terminator; each listed job except the unit's job word (+0x24), 93, 161 and 164 gives one output entry: the job row's skillset byte as a word, or the 8-byte entry (job, skillset).

the Secondary choices of the ability screen are Unit_CollectJobSkillsets' output in g_MenuList (sub_140366FE0, tab 1, through JobAbilityList_Build with tab 0 and mode 1); the pair list goes into g_JobAbilityPairList (JobScreen_BuildTabList, tab 1) and into JobScreen_FindJobOfSkillset's 146-entry frame list, both through JobScreen_BuildJobTabRows with tab 0 and mode 1.
g_MenuList is 256 words and the stock builders stop at 145 entries; g_JobAbilityPairList and the frame list hold 146 entries of 8 bytes (both initialised as 146 entries).

notes: The 145-entry limit is the game's list size (g_MenuList is shared with every shop and equip list; the frame list cannot grow in place).
open_questions: ? not run in the game: the Secondary list with more entries than a screenful (scrolling, choosing a late entry's skillset, the job shown for it); ? the other 24-word job lists (JobScreen_FillUnitRows' word_14375F800, sub_1400DCFE4's word_143CDAAE0, JobChange_FillUnitEntry's frame list) still end at 23 entries.

name: SettingsCloseSavesSystemFile
scope: what closing the settings screen writes
summary: Closing the settings screen requests a settings save, and the save rewrites the SYSTEM save file with the settings and the save manager's bytes +656..+895, among them the game-cleared byte.

behavior.text: `g_ConfigData` (0x140C69690, a pointer) +224 = a settings save requested, +225 = settings changed; 0x1400B5E24 (its per-frame step) does, when +224: if +225 and no save request is busy, `Options_ApplyBlock(g_SaveManager, block)` (0x1400C3814) with the settings and `g_SaveManager` +656..+895 (the game-cleared byte +888 among them), then +224 = +225 = 0; without +225 only +224 is cleared. `Options_ApplyBlock` names the 'SYSTEM' save (string xref 0x1400C3962). I: this writes the system save file.
the General Options on-close handler sets +224 = 1 unconditionally (0x140189057).
closing the screen rewrote the system save file within the same second, with the cleared byte as it was in memory (so +225 was set then; what set it was not read).

name: SixteenColourLimitIsTwoCpuBuilders
summary: The 15 colours of a unit sheet (16 with the transparent one) are a property of two CPU routines that expand 4-bit pixels through 16 converted colours; both hand the GPU 32-bit textures, and the battle one already has an 8-bit, 256-colour branch.

behavior.text: menus: CharaRender_BuildAtlasTexture reads the sheet entry, converts 16 colours and writes a 512 x 512 buffer of 32-bit texels for TextureObj_SetSource.
battle: HdLayer_BuildTextures reads the entry into a sheet group and HdGroup_BuildPiece expands a piece through the converted colours into 32-bit texels; its pixel width argument is 4 or 8.
the game itself uses the 8-bit branch with 256 colours for the sheet groups 15 to 17.

the HD sheet entries are 512 pixels wide at 4 bits (131072 bytes for 512 rows, 118784 for 464); the buffers they are read into hold 0x100000 bytes (menus) and 0x80000 bytes (a sheet group), so an 8-bit entry of the same size in pixels (262144 and 237568 bytes) fits both.

name: SkillsetIdsPastTheByte
summary: A skillset id is one byte everywhere the game keeps it (job row +0, unit +0x12 / +0x13 / +0x192, save A+7, the action's command byte +0x1A1, the battle menu arrays, the command table).

behavior.text: 242 sites; the 8-bit tests (17 monster range tests, the job rule 5..0x17, 0xE0, 0x18, 0x14, 7 / 8, the 0xFF terminators); the uses as an identity are the set arguments of Skillset_GetAbility / BuildAbilityList / BuildTabAbilityList / FindJobBySkillset, the g_CommandKind index, the name and help tokens 0xB000 / 0x9800 + set, equality tests of two sets, and stores of a whole id into a byte.

name: SkillsetNamesAndHelpAreKeyedBySetId
summary: A skillset's name and help are found by the set id alone: the name token is 0xB000 | set (text kind 22) and the help token 0x9800 | set (kind 19), both 11-bit indexes; the name row is the JobCommand-en NXD row keyed by the set as a 32-bit value, so a set of 0x800 or more spills into the kind bits.

behavior.text: nine producers add 0xB000 to a set (sub_140227CF8, BattleMsg_UnitTurnScene 0x14023750F, sub_1402EB408 0x1402EB489, sub_14022AFEC, sub_1402E1C64, sub_1402F9F20, sub_14032F410, sub_14032F9F8, sub_14033A37C); the resolver sub_140226208 (and EventText_FindMessage at 0x1402DDBEA) sends a token whose top five bits are 0x16 to the text slot object 9 and masks the index with 0x7FF.

sub_1401560D0 reads the same token as `token - 0xB000` (no mask) and takes the title from JobCommandTable_GetRow(set), the JobCommand-en table (41) row keyed by the set as an unsigned 32-bit value (JobCommandTable_GetRow, 14 call sites); it does not test the row for null.

the help token 0x9800 | set has four producers: sub_140301ED8 (0x1403020F1, adds to the word at word_14186AF1E), sub_140366ABC (0x140366D1F), sub_140366FE0 (0x1403671A3, the flags above the index are removed later) and a shared help slot; the resolver masks the same 0x7FF, and the stock help pool holds 227 strings.

notes: Source: IDA reads of 2026-11-12. The pool contents themselves were not read.
open_questions: ? the help text's reader for a set of 0x800 or more outside the three producers listed.

name: SoundCuesAreRemappedBeforeTheyPlay
summary: Every sound cue goes through SoundCue_Play, which first remaps it with IdRemap_Lookup (table g_IdRemapPairs, 406 rows of 7 from/to pairs) and drops any result above 0x2B1. Large cue ids (the effect bank values, e.g. 0x730000 for the Potion chime) are playable only through that table.

behavior.text: IdRemap_Lookup passes ids up to 0xA7 through; above that it walks rows of 56 bytes from g_IdRemapPairs and compares the row pointer with the address after the table (lea at 0x1402BA9FD) to stop; a match returns the pair's 'to' dword (-1 = no sound), no match returns the id.
SoundCue_Play returns -1 without playing when the remapped cue is above 0x2B1; an unremapped effect cue (0x73xxxx) is always above it.

a battle effect's sound events reach SoundCue_Play from EffectScript_OpRunTimeline with cue = track value + dword_14114B124 - 1; the stock Potion sends 0x730000 (remapped to 0x137, plays) and 0x730001 (remapped to -1, nothing).

open_questions: ? which other cue ranges besides the effect bank depend on the remap rows (event and UI cues below 0xA8 pass through).

name: SpawnedUnitsCarryAOneByteJob
summary: A spawned unit's job is one byte of its spawn record (+10), copied into the work record's job byte; the scripted-battle table OverrideEntryData has a 32-bit MainJob column, but the copy keeps only its low byte. The engine keeps the job in one byte there, so it cannot carry a job id above 255 to a spawned unit.

behavior.text: UnitWork_InitFromSpawnRecord loads the spawn record's byte +10 (0x140276B04) into the work record's job byte C +3 (0x140276B07) and then calls UnitWork_ApplyJobRow.
OverrideEntry_FillUnitEntry stores row dword +0x10 (MainJob), when it is not 0, as one byte into its 40-byte unit entry at +10: 300 becomes 44.
Unit_ApplySpawnRecord writes 0xFF into C +2 on one of its branches (0x1402763FB); C +2 is the save index (54 entries).

the 40-byte unit entries of OverrideEntry_LoadBattleEntries are spawn records: Battle_BuildEntryUnits passes the battle's entry block (Battle_GetEntryBlock) to it, so the rows overwrite the entries in place, and Battle_PlaceEntryUnits builds battle unit i from entry i with Unit_BuildFromRecord, giving it row i as the fifth argument (flow ScriptedBattleUnitsFromEntries).

notes: Stock rows of OverrideEntryData use MainJob values 2, 154 and 169..173 (checked against every stock row), all below 256, so the byte cast changes no stock unit.
open_questions: ? whether an event command can change a spawned unit's job (no opcode that carries a job id was found).

name: SpawnRecordPassiveWords
summary: A battle spawn record's reaction / support / movement word below 0x1FE names an ability and 0x1FE or above asks for a random one of the unit's skillset slots 16..21.

behavior.text: Unit_BuildRsmAbilityList returns a word below 0x1FE as is; otherwise it gathers the unit's slot ids 16..21 per job and keeps them by stock ranges (R 422..453, S 454..485, M >= 486).

Unit_InitAbilitiesFromJob puts the record's three words into the unit's learn queue only when below 0x1FE (three compares sharing dx = 0x1FE), then calls Unit_BuildRsmAbilityList for each (masks 2, 4, 8) and stores the answers at work +0x14 / +0x16 / +0x18.
sub_1401EA638 copies an OverrideEntryData row's reaction / support / movement (row +0x20 / +0x24 / +0x28) to the spawn entry's +0x0C / +0x0E / +0x10 as u16.

name: SpriteLookupFailuresPastTheTables
summary: What went wrong in game when a sprite number or job id above the stock range reached a reader: three failures.

behavior.text: a sprite number of 0xAA or more in the battle map's unit queue builder (sub_1403041A4, bound at 0x140304207) drew the unit as sprite 1 (the main character).

the sprite row table of the NXD table 0xAE (looked up with the sprite as key, 15 callers) has no rows above 169; the formation code in sub_140216EB4 read the row's byte at +0x2C from a null row (0x140217172) and crashed placing a unit of sprite 212.

a job id at or above the guard of the job menu list (the immediate 0xAE at 0x140286759, 0x140286803) took the null-row fallback and crashed when the second job page opened (access violation at 0x140286826). The guard at 0x140286759 is in Unit_CollectJobSkillsets, not in a list builder.

name: SpriteNumberStoreWidths
summary: Which stores of a unit's sprite number are bytes and which are wider: the battle path keeps the number in bytes (limit 255) while the menu path carries it as a 32-bit value.

behavior.text: byte stores: the return value of Unit_ResolvePreviewShape, the unit field +0x18F and +0x190, the scene-unit field +0xA, both leading bytes of a look pool record, the argument of CharShape_ApplyClut, the job row bytes +46 (own sprite number) and +47 (palette byte), the roster record marker.

a roster record's first byte below 0x80 is the sprite number itself; 0x80 and 0x81 mean 'generic man or woman' (look from the job byte), 0x82 'own look from the job row', 0xA2, 0xA3, 0xA5 and 0xA6 to 0xA9 fixed looks, other values the job id plus 40.
the load queue holds the sprite as a 16-bit word but LookQueue_Add replaces a signed value of 170 or more by 1 (the cmp is signed, so values above 32767 also pass as non-negative).

the menu sprite record keeps the sprite as a 32-bit value at +4 and the renderer slot cache as a 32-bit value; CharaRender_BuildAtlasTexture compares it unsigned with 0xA9 and the attribute reads in CharaRender_SetSlotRequest use its low 16 bits.
UnitWork_ApplyJobRow copies job row +46 and +47 to unit +0x18F and +0x190; that is the one data-driven sprite number the game has (a unit with marker 0x82 draws it).

name: SpriteSheetPortraitAndPartFiles
scope: engine (sprite sheet, classic file and portrait files)
summary: A unit sprite is two HD sheet entries plus a classic file whose first 0x200 bytes are its palettes; a portrait is a texture plus a part file that the game asks for by name.

behavior.text: an HD sheet is the pair of g2d.dat entries named by exe.sprite.hd_entry_by_shape row L and the next; the game loads each with sub_1403D2450(g2d, n, n + 1) and PackFile_ReadEntry(g2d, n, out), which inflates it (a 16-byte YOX block header, then zlib). A generic job's pair is 131072 + 118784 bytes inflated (512 x 512 and 512 x 464, 4 bpp).

the palette the sheet is drawn with is the first 0x200 bytes (16 palettes of 16 BGR555 colours) of the classic sprite file named by exe.sprite.classic_kind row L (file number, size), read by GameData_ReadSectors.
a portrait is ui/ffto/common/face/texture/wldface_<F>_<c>_uitx.tex plus the part file textureparts/wldface_<F>_<c>_uitx.utexpt that names it.

an HD sheet is the classic 256 x 488 sheet at twice the size in both directions, rows 0..255 in the first entry and 256..487 in the second, 4 bpp with the left pixel in the low nibble: a PlayStation-format sprite with every pixel doubled drew correctly.

behavior.basis: (format of a .utexpt part file, stock icon and face files)
behavior.text: +0 the texture path's offset P, +8 the part count n, n records of 20 bytes from +0x0C (name offset relative to the record, x0, y0, x1, y1; record 0 is the whole texture), P = 0x0C + 20 n, then the NUL-terminated path and the part names.

notes: Not yet seen: a sheet of another size, the classic graphics mode.
open_questions: ? what else reads a classic file (classic graphics mode draws the classic sheet itself); ? whether any reader bounds a g2d entry number.

name: SpriteSheetsAndClassicFilesByNumber
summary: HD sprite sheets are read by number and the loader accepts any number; classic sprite files are read by name only.

behavior.text: the sheet loader entries 0x1403D2450 (load), 0x1403D25D8 (decode) and 0x1403D25A4 (unload) accept any number, so a file named tex_<N>.bin under system/ffto/g2d is served for N above 2449, past the game's own table of contents.
classic files are mapped only by names already in the game's file list, so a name at an empty number is ignored (see EnhancedDrawsHdSheetsWithTheClassicFilePalette).
the first-sheet row of sprite 164 is 1120, so the sprite tables hold the entry numbers of the game's own g2d container directly (its table has 2450 entries, see sprites.md).

name: SpriteTablesCanLiveInBlocksOf1300Rows
summary: The game reaches every table indexed by a look number only through a fixed set of instructions and bounds.

behavior.text: the census of every code operand and data pointer into the ten tables finds 52 readers that address them (24 attribute, 7 HD, 2 per classic table, 1 per portrait copy and 2 for the shared one, 11 for the face table), no data pointer, and two operands that only look like readers (UnitFaceIndexReadsTheTableAfterTheHdTable and a byte table that starts at the last row of the copy at 0x140681A90).

the bounds that compare a look number before a table read are 32-bit immediates of compares or of loads compared as 16-bit words (0xA9 three times, 0xAA once, 0xD3 six times, 0x9F eleven times); the four HD compares on the scene unit's sprite byte (+0xA against 0xAA) are byte immediates.

out of range the stock readers fall back to a value a row can hold: -1 for the HD readers (they test the entry against -1), 0 for the six portrait readers (their code register is zeroed at entry), and for the face table the fixed list of SpriteId_ToShape (codes 176, 183, 188 to 201 and 205 name themselves, every other code -1).

name: SpriteTablesEndAtSprite169
summary: The tables indexed by sprite number all have 170 rows (sprites 0 to 169); the unit queue and the face readers compare against fixed bounds, so a sprite number above 169 needs every table and every bound to grow.

behavior.text: the HD sheet table at 0x1407151F0 holds a signed 32-bit first-sheet number per sprite (-1 = none; the second sheet is the next number); sprites 155 to 158 are -1, sprite 159 is 1110, sprite 164 is 1120, sprite 169 is 1130.

the classic file table at 0x140784690 and its twin at 0x140784BE0 hold a file number and a size per sprite (8 bytes a row); sprites 87 to 92 and 96 share one file, 93 has its own, 155 to 158 are empty, 159 to 162 are 880 to 883 (the Dark Knight and Onion Knight pair of the handheld edition), 164 to 169 are 885 to 890. The twin matches the first table in the rows read.
the sprite attribute table at 0x140673300 has 4 bytes a row and its row 170 already holds other data, so a sprite above 169 reads the neighbouring table.

three word tables hold the classic portrait code per sprite at 0x140680070, 0x140683A70 and 0x1406807C0 (211 entries); rows 164 to 169 are 0 and rows 203 to 209 hold 0x71 to 0x77. Two readers compare the index with 0xD3 and take a no-code path above it (0x14032AC18 in sub_14032AB3C, 0x1402C0848 in Unit_GetSpriteSetId).
the unit queue builder sub_1403041A4 loads 0xAA at 0x140304207 and compares the sprite number with it (jump if less).
the other fixed bounds are 0xA9 or 0xAA at the HD sheet readers (0x1400CE263, 0x140261714, 0x1402617A4, 0x1402618EC, 0x14026C335, 0x14026F006, 0x14026F02D).

name: StatusBitWritersAndTheRemovalPath
summary: The effective set +0x61 of a unit is written at the end of a fixed group of functions; the applied set is written only from the pending sets, from its own saved copy or derived from +0x61; the game removes a status only through the pending remove.

behavior.text: the writers of +0x61 in battle are the tails of Battle_StatusApply, Battle_StatusRefresh, Unit_ReinitStatusCountdowns, Unit_BuildInnateStatuses and its Ex twin, Unit_SetChargeStateBits (byte 0), sub_14030D1CC (byte 0), BTurn_PreviewAction, the clear-all branch of Battle_ApplyActionResult, the unit builders, and the whole-set copies back of the event restore and the AI.

the applied set is written only from the pending sets (Battle_StatusApply / Refresh), from its own saved copy (Unit_BuildInnateStatuses, the event restore) or derived from +0x61 by Unit_InitBattleStatusState, whose callers build the record just before; stock countdowns tick only for applied bits (Battle_TurnEngine phase 4).
the tail of Battle_StatusResolve sets +5 bit 3 and the side bits from +0x61.
the game removes a status only through the pending remove, which Status_FilterPendingSets cuts to applied & ~innate a.

name: StatusesAreFortyBitSetsInEightRegions
summary: A unit's statuses are 40-bit sets (status s = bit 0x80 >> (s & 7) of byte s >> 3) kept in eight regions of the battle unit record: innate a, innate b, the effective set, the applied set, the pending add and remove pair, 16 countdown bytes for the statuses 24..39, and the KO counter. Nothing is saved. The code is written to this shape in about 1,000 places: fixed loops of 40, fixed five-byte copies, and fixed bytes and masks that name one status each.

behavior.text: the effective set is always innate a OR applied; the three loops of Resolve (filter, refresh, apply) are the only code that sets or clears applied bits for combat; events and previews copy sets wholesale.
23 compares against 40 or 39 over status ids in 20 functions, 190 literal-mask tests naming 38 statuses in 102 functions, 10 computed-bit sites, about 240 fixed five-byte or 16-byte accesses.

the immunity sets (+58, +63, +68), remove mask (+466) and fourth group (+408) are the same bytes as innate a, innate b, the effective set and the applied set seen through the result block base; they are not separate regions.
the property table is read with a 16-byte row, the group masks with a 5-byte row, the added-effect records with a 6-byte row, all indexed by status id below 40.

open_questions: ? untyped readers of the sets (about 51 candidate masks marked I in the census) need a live write-watch.

name: StatusLoopsInflictCopyAndBattleTableLifetime
summary: The status pipeline (Battle_StatusResolve) runs a filter, a refresh and an apply loop over the status ids in order; the inflict copy of a result is read only by formula 56; the battle task clears the unit table at its start and the battle capture copies it whole.

behavior.text: the game's filter, refresh and apply loops visit the status ids in order; the apply loop makes a per-status filter call.
Formula 56 is the only reader of the inflict copy at 0x1407B07B0 (Battle_ResolveAction writes it from g_InflictRecords).
the battle task marks every unit slot empty at its start (sub_140210AF0); Battle_SaveCapture and Battle_RestoreCapture copy the whole unit table.

name: StatusScreenReadersAndIconPath
summary: The battle Status screen lists a unit's statuses in two dword lists (gains, ailments) and reads each one's name, category, sort key and caption from its UIStatusEffect row (key id + 1); the icon path s_%03d is formatted with the status id.

behavior.text: the three UIStatusEffect readers refuse an id above 39 with one compare each.
the icon path s_%03d is formatted with the id.

name: StatusVisualMasks
summary: A scene unit carries set and clear masks for status visuals; SceneUnit_ApplyStatusVisuals applies them and redraws the pose, and a scene unit build zeroes the words.

behavior.text: scene unit +0x15C..+0x170 are the status visual words: +0x15C = +0x164 | +0x15C & ~+0x16C and +0x160 = +0x168 | +0x160 & ~+0x170 (set masks +0x164 / +0x168, clear masks +0x16C / +0x170); the masks are cleared afterwards.

+0x15C bits 0x1FFFC2C4 make the apply step set +0x370 (a pose flag); +0x160 bits 0..3 select the effect sprites 155..158 and bits 7 / 8 a pending transform (0x100 = sprite 146, the chicken / frog sprite).

SceneUnit_SyncSpriteFromPool (from the apply step) sets the scene unit's sprite byte back to its pool record's +1 when no effect sprite (155..158) is shown, taking the saved frame tables (+0x230 / +0x238).

name: StockFormulaHandlersAreBlockSequences
summary: The 106 stock formula handlers are plain functions with no arguments over the frame Battle_ResolveAction sets up; 47 of them are sequences of the game's own building blocks.

behavior.text: the 106 stock handlers are plain functions with no arguments over the frame Battle_ResolveAction sets up (caster, target, result block R, formula block); 47 are block sequences only; the blocks are themselves plain functions (no arguments but the element affinity block's element in cl); a gate returns 1 and a failed roll clears R+0 when the action misses.

name: StockJobRowData
summary: Facts about the stock job rows of job.en, generaljob and jobtype: unused rows still carry numbers, the generic jobs map to texture part indices, and Ramza's jobs share the Squire's job type.

Those rows still hold numbers (an `exe.job` row, a `jobtype` id, a `jobcommand` id, a `TexturePartsIndex`), e.g. row 56: job type 34 (the Mystic's), command 16 (the Mystic's), texture parts 12. name: StoryChoiceBalloon
scope: story scenes: a dialogue balloon with several selectable lines
summary: A choice balloon is an ordinary message whose text contains the control code 0xFB (options start on this line) and 0xFC (run the choice). Each frame the message window task focuses one of two option nodes of the event window and shows the finger cursor, moves the cursor with up / down, and on confirm stores the 0-based index in event variable 24; the event script branches on it. No opcode and no message flag is involved. Seen live at the Mandalia opening: that choice is not skippable and fast-forward does nothing.

behavior.text: authoring: code 0xFB stores the current line number as the first option row (0xFFFF = none); code 0xFC runs the choice loop; with no 0xFB before it the 0xFC does nothing (EventMessage_Task and EventMessage_Scripted byte switches). Opcode 0x10 only starts the window.

the choice loop runs one frame at a time: it calls sub_1401365AC and sub_140136654 (next bullets), waits one frame, leaves on task tag 3 or word_142FEC554, else reads action 0x21 (up, mask 0x1000), 0x22 (down, mask 0x4000), 0x1A (confirm, mask 0x20) with Input_TestAction on g_EventButtonMask1. Cancel (0x1B) is not read; no fast-forward or auto-advance test is in the loop.

the cursor starts on the first option row, up stops at it, down stops at the last line reached so far (option count = last line - first option row + 1, I). The digits '1.' and '2.' are plain message text. Seen live 2026-11-09: DOWN moved the cursor from option 1 to option 2, UP moved it back, and the cursor does not wrap.

the UI path (code, both functions read in full in IDA): each frame sub_1401365AC(event agent, window variant, window size, cursor) takes the option node of the event window selected by the cursor (an option node exists for the cursor values 0 and 1 only; a larger value does nothing) and gives it the input focus through GUICore_FocusNode; sub_140136654(event agent) then shows the finger cursor with UIAgentCursor_Show when the window's six node pointers are all set. So this build has two option nodes per choice window.

while the choice waits the focused widget is the event window (ui/ffto/event/ffto_event.uib) and the finger cursor is shown, at (575, 183) on option 1 and (575, 235) on option 2 (52 px per line). After the confirm the next balloon of the same event keeps that focus but has no finger cursor, and an ordinary balloon of a battle opening never showed one. Recognition used by the tools: the focused widget is the event window AND the finger cursor is shown.

the balloon ran in the first task table (slot 2 of the table at 0x140D40AA0): task entry EventMessage_Task, block +0x90 = 1, tag 1. The second table (0x14184B3C0) had no running entry. The text id at block +8 (0x49435, kind 18, index 1077) points at an unrelated pool string: the drawn text is the event window's own text node, so scanning the pool string of the running task does NOT find the choice and is not a recognition.

on confirm the task writes cursor - first option row to dword 24 of the event variable store (off_1407830D8 and g_EventWorkPtr both point to 0x140D40060): event variable 24 at 0x140D40078; sound id 1 on confirm, 3 on a cursor move. Seen live 2026-11-09: pad A confirmed (three times); variable 24 read 0 before and 0 after choosing option 1, so that case does not show the write; option 2 was not chosen (it changes the battle's objective).

at this choice the skip gate read: event script running 1, armed 0, veto 0, skip state 0, skip-once 0 = not skippable; a skip request did nothing and a held fast-forward did nothing (3 runs, the hold lasted until stopped by hand). By the code EventSkip_IsAvailable has no message or choice test, so whether a choice can be skipped depends only on armed per event (0 at this one).

while skip runs (word_142FEC554, or g_EventSkipEnabled with the skip state set) the task replaces every text byte by 0xFE, so a choice is passed unanswered and variable 24 keeps its old value (code; not seen live because the Mandalia choice cannot be skipped).
fast-forward (RB / Ctrl) and auto-advance act only in the ordinary page wait loop, never on a waiting choice (code; seen live 2026-11-09: a held fast-forward did nothing at the choice).

a normal balloon page wait is a different loop (codes 0xFE / 0xFD, tests 0x1A, 0x1B, 0x20, 0x39, up / down only to scroll). dword_140D4081C is set in both loops by the code, but read live it was 0 on every read while the choice waited (2026-11-09, two tools, several reads): it is not usable as a 'waiting' flag from outside the game thread.

the 584-byte glove sprite records at 0x142FEF870 stayed hidden (x = 512) and nothing in those records, the task blocks or the event globals changed when DOWN moved the cursor: this build draws the cursor through the UI, so the sprite record y is NOT the cursor.

notes: Detail and evidence: the function sheets linked from this page (EventMessage_Task, EventMessage_Scripted, sub_1401365AC, sub_140136654). Live results of 2026-11-09 (Mandalia Plain opening, event 16) are tagged in the bullets.
open_questions: ? Where the task's 0xFB / 0xFC text bytes come from for this balloon (the pool string at the text id is unrelated; the drawn text is the event window node). ? What option 2 writes to event variable 24 (only option 1 was chosen: 0 before and after). ? Whether keyboard Enter confirms (only pad A tried). ? A choice outside a battle (world or town event). ? A choice with more than two options (the UI call handles the cursor values 0 and 1 only). ? Which opcodes read variable 24 afterwards.

name: StoryEventListBuildsASharedBoardArrayFromBitVariablesAndHoldsTextReferences
scope: engine (tavern list pages, story event list)
summary: A list of replayable story events has 78 entries: 64 plain ones that read event variables 444 to 507 and 14 special ones that read 427 to 440 (only 430, 433 and 440 can be listed); a listed entry is a 16-bit text reference (bank 29, message index 0 to 77) appended to a 128-entry array that other tavern lists share; the confirm starts the story event named by a 78-word table indexed by the message index.

behavior.text: the builder walks positions 0 to 77; the positions 14, 16, 28, 33, 47, 61, 62, 63, 64, 65, 66, 75, 76 and 77 are special (a chain of compares with constants) and read event variable 427 plus their own count; the other 64 read 444 plus theirs. All of these are single-bit variables (the variable space has 32-bit cells below 128, bits from 128 to 863 and nibbles from 864 to 1023).

an entry is listed when its variable is nonzero and the helper that hides eleven special variables (427, 428, 429, 431, 432, 434 to 439) says no; the list item is the variable number minus 6588 (plain, 0xE800 plus 0 to 63) or minus 6507 (special, 0xE840 plus 0 to 13) as an unsigned 16-bit value.

an item is a text reference: bits 11 to 15 name the text bank (29) and bits 0 to 10 the message index; the page text is the message index plus 59392, and the confirm reads the event number from the table at 0x1407B81B0 with the message index (a 16-bit read; entry 67 holds 0xFFFF, no event).

the builder stores each item in the array at 0x140D498F0 and a zero in the parallel array at 0x140D497D0 (128 words each) with a range check at a byte offset of 0x100; the same two arrays are addressed by 26 functions (34 and 18 operands, one function a gap chunk of the function table): the tavern list builders, the errand board code and the list widget, whose state keeps the array's address.

every builder that stores into the arrays checks the byte offset with an imm32 compare against 0x100 followed by a jump to __report_rangecheckfailure (14 of them, in 13 functions), Errand_BuildActiveList checks the element index against 0x80, and the level-list builder (sub_140375AD0) compares with r12 = 0x100, the same register that forms its bank-30 text reference.

the entry page reads row 67 (0xFFFF) into variable 39 as 65535 and EventChain_Find misses; no retail script writes variable 430 with the arithmetic opcodes (I: byte pattern of opcodes 0xB0..0xBE over the 560 retail scripts, which find every plain variable 444..507 set once with 0xBE then 0xB0 1) and no exe instruction loads 430 as an EventVar_Write argument, so the entry is never listed in the retail game.
the entry page also shows the text reference 0x8800 plus the index (bank 17), so an entry has a message in bank 29 (its label) and one in bank 17 (its page).
the list widget keeps a signed 16-bit cursor and two 16-bit count fields; the confirm writes event variable 508 = 1 and variable 39 = the event number and starts the event.
the builder's only callers are EventViewer_EntryPage and sub_140375538, both run as tasks of the in-engine task dispatcher sub_140246078 (called from Game_MainLoop).

a software tracepoint on the builder had 0 hits while the tavern's Rumors list and the main menu's Chronicle > Events list were opened and reopened; both of those screens are built from another source.

notes: Earlier readings of 17 special entries (427 to 443) and 61 plain ones (444 to 504) were wrong: the counts are 14 and 64.
open_questions: ? which screen of the Enhanced UI (if any) starts the in-engine tasks that show this list; ? the resource file behind bank 29 (resource slots 10 and 12) and bank 17; ? the events of the other special entries and why they are hidden; ? how the special variables 433 and 440 are set (no retail script writes 427..440 with the arithmetic opcodes).

Each errand then has its own test (town, story variable 111, prerequisite, delay, state).

name: TavernRumoursListGossipRowsByIdTownMaskAndUnlockVariable
summary: The tavern's Rumors list holds the nxd Gossip rows whose ids pass an availability test: ids 0..63 are walked; an id is listed when its Gossip row exists, its condition is met, and either its Gossip flag is set or the town's bit is set in a 64-entry mask table and event variable 721 + id is nonzero.

the list entry is the Gossip key (a dword), so the widget reads the row's title and text by the full id.

name: TexelWeights8Bit
scope: GPU (the test machine's GPU and driver)
summary: Bilinear filtering weights are the sub-texel fraction rounded to 1/256 (8 bits), not exact: the filtered colour of a texel pair at fraction f uses round(f * 256) / 256.

behavior.text: with 1/256 px vertex snapping, rounded 1/256 weights give 99.4 % exact; truncated 1/256 weights 92.7 %, 1/512 weights 93.2 %, exact weights 93.5 %.
the precision of the filtered result itself does not matter (rounding it to 1/(255 * 256) changes one value of 10076; coarser rounding is worse).
other GPUs (vendors, drivers) may use other weight precisions: a viewer that matches this machine byte for byte may differ by 1 elsewhere, as the game itself does.

name: TextFillPassDrawnAsOneShape
scope: UI text (SDF font runs: the screen title, the job name tag, the level boards)
summary: A text run's fill pass reaches its target as one shape: the fill glyphs are drawn without blending under a depth test (LESS_EQUAL, depth = 1 - the distance at the pixel centre), so where neighbouring glyph quads overlap the glyph with the largest distance keeps the pixel; the result is composited once. The shadow pass is blended glyph by glyph.

behavior.basis: (code, function SDFFontRenderer_Flush and the five program entries of shader/SDFFont.tec)
behavior.text: the glyph pass with program 1 has blending off and depth test + write LESS_EQUAL, the fill pixel shader is the only one that writes SV_Depth (= 1 - d); the glyph pass with program 0 blends straight alpha without depth. I: program 1 is the fill and program 0 the shadow (shader lists in file order).
choosing the winner by the centre distance (a later glyph on a tie) gives the same frames as choosing by the most coverage.

behavior.basis: (frame t4, the 'Squire' name tag: every draw of the tag layer replayed offline against the capture)
behavior.text: per-glyph blending 0.084 mean / max 33 at the touching serifs of u-i, r-e, q-u; the run's fill as one shape with the maximum coverage per pixel 0.011 / max 2 (the shadows too as one shape) and in the studio 0.004 / max 1 with the shadows per glyph.

behavior.basis: (studio, the three text regions of frame t4 and the Archer frame)
behavior.text: fills as one shape, shadows per glyph: title 0.056 / max 18 -> 0.034 / max 1, name tag 0.101 / max 33 -> 0.004 / max 1, Lv board 0.083 -> 0.081, chips 0.037 -> 0.036; Archer frame name tag 0.057 -> 0.015. Worse: the shadows as one shape as well (title 0.086), the fills blended with a MAX operation (title 1.07), the first or the last glyph winning an overlap (> 1.6), the maximum taken on the distances before the coverage curve (title 0.049, tag 0.050 / max 23).

open_questions: ? where the fill target is composited (program 2's quad is issued before the batch's glyph draws in SDFFontRenderer_Flush); ? the depth format.

name: TextLanguage
scope: the text language: where it comes from, where it is read, how the text files are chosen
summary: How the game picks and applies its text language.

behavior.text: the current text language is the u32 at `g_LanguageInfo` (0x143CD9B10) + 8 (registry TextLanguageCodes); it is read in `ResourceHandle_FinishLoad` and `EventEndSlate_ShowTask`.
the first value at start: `sub_14002851C` takes the Windows user locale, then Steam's `GetCurrentGameLanguage` (japanese, english, french, german, schinese, tchinese, koreana) when Steam answers.
after `settings.sav` loads, `sub_1401E7EF8` sets +8 from `g_ConfigData[21] & 0x1F` (the saved text language; the voice language is the next byte). Bit 7 of that byte is not decoded (?).
the Settings option table `ConfigItemTextLanguage` has 7 rows; a chosen code is validated by `sub_14002BCE0` (case 7 of `sub_140189D54`).

a localized resource key carries the language in a nibble (`+8 & 0xF`); the text nxd files come from the packs `data/enhanced/0004.<lang>.pac`; handles flagged localized (flag 8) are walked when the language changes.

a change of Text Language (Enhanced) in General Options reloads the text nxd tables at once, without a restart (the menus redraw in the new language; a shop list showed the new language's item names).

the text language is set only in General Options on the mode select screen (Language tab: Text Language (Enhanced), Text Language (Classic), Voice Language); the in-game Settings has no language option.
`root.nxl` lists each nxd table once, so every language's file of one table shares one table id.
the 53 text tables have the same columns, keys, row size and table id in all seven languages (`<name>.<lang>.nxd` decodes with the English layout).

name: TextNodeDrawGate
summary: GUITextNode_Draw returns before drawing unless a byte at node +0xCC is non-zero, a byte at +0x91 is zero, the string size at +0xE8 is non-zero and a font-table / font-set lookup returns true. Draw is still called for a node that fails the gate, so a call is not evidence that text was drawn.

behavior.text: the four tests run in that order and a failure jumps to the end of the function before any glyph is emitted.
the font test calls sub_1403DBA94(font table, node +0x12C); the string size is the qword at +0xE8, and the two bytes are +0xCC and +0x91 (decompile).

notes: V: the gate runs at the top of the function, so a closed gate also skips the palette upload and the batch flush the body would do.
open_questions: ? which writer clears +0xCC and sets +0xE8 on the banner's Title node.

name: TextReferenceIsABankAndAnElevenBitIndex
summary: An event message is named by a 16-bit reference: the top five bits select one of 32 text banks (each a resource), the low 11 bits are the message index inside it; the lookup counts message terminators from the start of the bank, so its cost grows with the index.

behavior.text: bank = (reference >> 11) and 0x1F, pointer = the bank table entry at 0x14184A8A0 + 8 x bank; bank 14 and bank 22 (0xB000) are fetched from resource slots; the others are read from the pointers the loaders set (sub_14032A8A0 and the screens that load their own text).

the message is found by stepping through the bytes of the bank and counting terminator codes (bytes 0xFE and 0xFF) until the count equals the message index (reference and 0x7FF); a bank holds at most 2,048 messages by this rule.
callers pass 16-bit values (list items are 16-bit words); no caller was seen passing a wider reference.

notes: The errand board and the tavern lists store these references as their list items.
open_questions: ? which banks hold which screens' text (banks 3, 4, 5, 10, 16, 21 and 26 have no static writer).

name: TitleAndSaveListScreens
scope: title screens, Continue / Load Game save list
summary: The screens between launch and a loaded game, the keys they take, and how the save list is built, as seen live.

behavior.text: after a launch the first focused screen is ffto_title_mode_select.uib (Enhanced / Classic); A on Start Game leads to the opening narration screens with no focused widget; the title menu (ffto_title_enhanced.uib: New Game, Continue, Load Game, Select Version, 50 px apart) appears by itself after about 33 s.
the title takes the keyboard without a pad-mode switch: Space skips the narration (scene becomes title), Enter then shows the menu within about 3 s.
the cursor starts on New Game (glove y 866; Continue 917, Load Game 965); Enter on New Game starts the first battle directly (no cutscene was seen).

Continue and Load Game both open ffto_system_saveload.uib. Each entry shows Auto or the slot number, a timestamp, the map, a place label (Pre-battle, Mid-battle, World Map), level, difficulty and chapter. Tabs: Manual Saves, Autosaves, All (default).

the list draws a window of five entries over a longer list (15 here: 10 manual, 5 auto) and scrolls; UP from the top wraps to the bottom; entries are 206 px apart. The list ignores input for about 2 s while it fades in, and fills in over a few reads (one entry first).

manual saves are the slots 1 to 10 and never rotate; autosaves rotate and world map activity (entering a settlement, leaving a shop) writes new ones, pushing Mid-battle autosaves out; a Pre-battle autosave of 11-03 stayed through all runs.

on the mode select screen the keyboard Enter on Start Game acts at once; the pad A is swallowed by the pad-mode switch (the first pad press only switches the input mode), so a pad press there costs a resend of about 5 s. The narration after it has no focused widget and reports a cinematic agent with skip allowed 0, but it IS skippable: Space then Enter skips it (the skip flag says nothing about keys). A key sent during the intro can be lost, so the press is repeated and varied by watching whether the state changed.

Esc on the save list returns to the title menu with the glove still on Continue (y 916). For under a second the focus is empty, which looks like the narration but is not; an input sent then (Space + Enter) pressed Continue again and reopened the list. The game also falls back to the narration by itself after the menu has idled for about 40 s.
E (keyboard) switches the save list tabs; after a switch the list refills over several reads, and a read taken right after the key can still show the old tab (wait for three equal reads).

notes: The opening logo videos were not observed.
