name: TitleBackdropAndInputFlag
scope: the title screen behind another screen
summary: Hiding the title add-on hides its backdrop; input reaches an add-on only when its byte +47 is clear.

behavior.text: writers of +47 in the title code: UIAddonFFTOTitlePlaymode vtable slot 17 (0 at 0x1401C5674) and 0x1401C60E4 (1 at 0x1401C6172). I: +47 = takes no input.
`GUIComponent_UpdateNodeTree` skips a node with enabled byte +144 = 0 with its whole subtree.

the title agent's own functions (UITitle_ShowMenu, UIAgentFFTOTitle_Update, UIAgentFFTOTitle_OnAddonEvent, UITitle_OnMenuAction, UITitle_ShowPlayMode) use their agent's +72 / +80 / +88, not the menu add-on's rows.

name: TitleMenuRows
scope: which rows the Enhanced title menu shows and how they are laid out
summary: The Enhanced title menu shows 3 to 6 rows chosen by the save state and the cleared flag; the layout file has a state for each count.

behavior.text: the menu has 3 to 6 rows: 4 for a game that is not cleared with a save (New Game, Continue, Load Game, Select Version), 6 for a cleared game with a save. The add-on holds six rows and the layout file has the states Menu3 to Menu6 only.
`g_UIStateFade` (0x143CD9E00) holds the fade timer (+16, the title's actions wait for it to reach 0 or less) and the requested state (+24); the title writes states 6 and 19.
`g_SaveManager` (0x143CD9EE0) +888 gates New Game + and Music Player (I: game cleared); +889 / +890 let the mode select start Classic / Enhanced at once.

name: TitleMenuRowStorage
scope: where the title add-on keeps its rows and what lies after them
summary: The title add-on stores six 24-byte rows at +72; the count, current row, last input tick and flags follow at +216..+230, and no instruction of the title code touches +231..+239, so a seventh row would overlap those fields.

behavior.text: `UIAddonFFTOTitle` is 240 bytes (`Mem_Alloc(240)` in UIAddonFFTOTitle_Create 0x1401CB9B4, +72..+215 and +216..+230 cleared): +64 the TitleEnhanced node; +72 six rows of 24 bytes {button node, text node, kind byte at +16}; +216 count, +220 current row, +224 last input tick, +228 a save exists, +229 cleared, +230 idle timeout armed.
a row's kind byte is read at +88 + 24 * index; row index 6 would have its kind byte at +232, its button node at +216 (the count) and its text node at +224 (the last input tick).
the +48 part (`UIFFTOMenuFunctionBase`) reads the row count and current row at its +168 / +172, which are the add-on's +216 / +220 (menu code shared with other menus).
the layout file has the row states Menu3..Menu6 only; GUINode_ApplyStateAtFrame with a name the file lacks (Menu7) changes nothing.

with seven rows set up, the title menu drew three rows: writing the node fields of the components returned by GUINode_FindDescendant does not move the rows (the parent's states animate the Reference parts).

name: TodaysCalendarDateIsHeldInEventVariables46And47
summary: The calendar's current month and day are event variables 46 (month 1..12) and 47 (day). The daily tick compares each tracked date with these two; event variables 95 and 96 hold a different date, the one slot 0 counts (the player's birthday).

behavior.text: the tick reads variable 0x2E (46) and variable 0x2F (47) through EventVar_Read and compares them with each slot's month and day (0x1402CD08D..0x1402CD0F2).

seen live, variables 46 / 47 advance with world-map travel (April 3 to April 5 on one trip, April 9 to April 11 on another), and a tracked counter rose by one on the trip that passed its date, also when the date was passed mid-trip.
seen live, variables 95 / 96 read January 1 on a New Game with the birthday January 1.

notes: Seen 2026-11-16 on the Steam PC build.

name: TrackedDateCountersAreCopiedBySixteenByteMovesInFiveSequences
summary: Outside the two counting loops, the 64 counter bytes are moved only by sequences of four 16-byte moves: the save pack and unpack, the checkpoint writer and reader, the battle capture's errand-state copy in both directions, and the new-game reset; all use aligned moves on the live block.

behavior.text: each sequence has four 16-byte moves of the live counters (movaps, so the live address is 16-byte aligned) interleaved with moves of other state; the checkpoint buffer holds its copy at 0x142E808DC and the battle capture buffer (0x1408B8588) at +0x2D4.

SaveWork_CopyErrandState has one body for both directions (its second argument 0 = live to capture, nonzero = capture to live); Battle_SaveCapture calls it with 0 and Battle_RestoreCapture with the restore flag; the capture buffer is one fixed global, so a restore reads whatever the buffer holds, including a buffer filled from a saved file.

the new-game reset (sub_14033FB84) writes the 64 bytes from a constant block of starting values at 0x1407BAC30 (not zero: it begins 16, 16, 15, 15, 28, 37, 37, 56) with four aligned stores; seen live: after the reset ran, all 64 counters equalled that block.
seen live, the reset runs when the game returns to the title (the counters read the starting values at the title); starting a New Game from the title does not run it again before the first battle.
the save pack stores the 64 bytes at +0x48C of the save copy (followed by the errand count at +0x4CC); the unpack reads them back.

open_questions: ? whether the checkpoint buffer is ever filled by a path other than the writer.

name: TrackedDateCountersAreCountedByTwoFunctionsAndShownByTheLevelListPage
summary: Each of 64 tracked date slots owns one counter byte (cap 99) in a 64-byte block; the daily calendar tick and the jump by N days count a slot when its date is reached; the page of the second tavern list prints the counter of the selected position; the block is saved and copied in seven places.

behavior.text: slot 0 compares event variables 95 and 96 with the current month and day, slots 1 to 63 compare the {month, day} byte pairs at 0x1407B8130; the daily tick adds 1 up to 99 on a match; the jump by N days adds the whole years passed and one for each date crossed, capped at 99.

a census of the whole image finds 41 operands of the counter block in 12 functions: the tick, the jump, the page of the second tavern list (the only reader, two read sites), and seven functions that copy or reset the 64 bytes (save pack and unpack at +0x48C of the save work block, the errand state copy twice, the checkpoint writer and reader, the reset).

the page reads counter[(selected entry) >> 4], where the entry is `level + 16 x position` built by sub_140375AD0 from the four-bit event variables 960 + position (positions 0 to 63 except 18, 21, 52 and 53); the entry is a bank 30 text reference; the page text is bank 17 message (low byte of the entry), where bank 17 is the loaded block `position / 16 + 6` of packed file 767 (a table of 114 sector offsets).
the three loop bounds over the 64 slots are imm8 compares (cmp reg, 40h) at 0x1402CD10E, 0x14039DBCE and 0x140375B7B.
for a slot whose pair is {0, 0} the jump function's day arithmetic gives -1 and increments the counter, so an unfilled slot would count.
a scan of the functions that take the address of the live block and index into it found no other reader (the scan cannot see a base held in a struct field).

notes: The earlier statement that no reader exists was wrong: the cross-reference list misses operands that use an image base register with a 32-bit displacement.
open_questions: ? the name of the screen that shows the level list; ? the file that holds packed file 767's blocks.

name: TrackedDateLoopsVisitEverySlotBelowTheirBoundAndTheJumpAddsTheYearsToEachOne
summary: The daily tick and the jump by N days walk the slots from 1 (the tick) or 0 (the jump) up to a bound of 64 and treat every slot they visit alike: the tick counts a slot whose pair equals today, the jump adds the whole years passed to every visited counter and one more when the slot's date lies inside the span; a visited slot with no date is counted by the jump.

behavior.text: the tick loop (0x1402CD0D6..0x1402CD112) reads the pair of slot rcx, compares month then day with today's month and day, and adds 1 to the counter below the cap of 99; the loop bound is a compare of rcx with 64 (an 8-bit immediate). Slot 0 is handled before the loop with event variables 95 and 96.

the jump loop (0x14039DB1F..0x14039DBD2) first adds the years passed (the day count divided by 365, truncated) to the counter as an 8-bit add, then, for slots 1 and up, reads the pair; its day of the year is the days before the month plus the day minus 1 (a month below 2 sums nothing); the slot counts one more when that day is not after the target day of the year (the current day of the year plus the remaining days, modulo 365) and its distance from the current day is below the remaining days; a counter above 99 is set to 99.
a slot with the pair {0, 0} gives the day of the year -1, which passes both tests: the jump counts it (checked by an emulated run of the loop).
a month above 12 would read past the 12-entry days-per-month table the loops sum (0x140680FF8), and there is no leap day in that table (February has 28 days).
the level list builder (0x140375B23..0x140375B7E) is a third loop with the same bound of 64 (a 32-bit compare of ebx), over positions 0..63.

notes: Tested by running the stock loops on a mapped copy of the image against an independent model of the arithmetic above.

name: TurnOrderEntryKeepsNineBitsOfTheAbility
summary: A turn-order entry keeps 9 bits of the pending ability (byte 1 plus bit 7 of byte 0 for 256), so the combat timeline names an ability of 512 or more by the stock ability 256 + its low byte (512 = Vengeance).

behavior.text: the tag and unit-panel decoders (TurnPanel_SetTag, TurnPanel_SetUnitPanel) and two more decoders build the timeline's name strings (Battle_TimelineBuildStrings 0x1403244FF, Battle_TimelineBuildStrings2 0x140364BD3: token 0x7000 + the decoded id).

name: UIAddonBaseEventRouting
scope: how a screen's events reach its handlers
summary: Every add-on's event handler calls UIAddon_OnEventBase first; input reaches the add-on's slot 12 only when its id is not excluded, byte +47 is clear and slot 3 allows it.

behavior.text: event 1 = input, 4 = per-frame update, 5 = shown, 6 = hidden, 7 = busy query, 0xC = focus a node, 13 = release a list (details on the sheet).
a screen hidden with `UIAddon_Hide` (0x1401D1EAC) sets +43 while it hides; slot 3 refuses input while +42 or +43 is set.

node events of the General Options rows: a switch node (kind 4 at +536, on flag at +648) posts event 21 / 22 to the add-on ids in its listener slots (+584, 4 slots); a list item node has kind 10 at +536.

name: UIStateClock
summary: How the clock of a UI state runs: real elapsed time per UI frame (never less than 1/60 s), summed in single precision, frame = time * 60.0 as a float; the end or a loop resets frame and time and drops the overshoot.

behavior.text: the application's frame limiter (App_RunFrame) waits until the elapsed frame time (ticks * scale / 300000.0, in double) reaches 1/60 s, so an application frame is never shorter than 1/60 s at scale 1; the step it stores for the frame is the elapsed time clamped by the timer's maximum step (timer +16, value not read).
the UI scene callers form dt = (float)(ticks * scale / 300000.0) from an object with the same two fields.
that object is the same frame timer, so UI_FrameUpdate's dt is the clamped application frame step.
UI_FrameUpdate multiplies dt by g_UIDataModule+28 (1.0 in the table the module is created with) and GUICore_BeginFrame stores it at g_GUICore+2100; a second value goes to +2104.
GUICore_TickWidget gives each widget dt = 0 while a block bit is set that the widget's mask lacks, else +2100 (widget selector 0) or +2104 (selector 1); other selector values skip the widget.

GUINodeState_Advance: time = (dt * rate) + time and frame = time * 60.0, both single precision; a state that reaches its end frame either loops (frame and time = range start, overshoot dropped) or stops on the end frame; a jump marker passed sets frame and time to its start frame the same way.
the sampled frame is the float, not an integer: only the key search truncates it; the position within a key interval uses the float.

at 60 Hz the frame advances by 1 plus a small excess per UI frame (the excess is the part of the real frame time above 1/60 s), so a 40-frame loop takes 40 UI frames; on a slow frame the clock jumps by more than one frame (real time is kept).

the live Loop frames carry fractions well above the single-precision excess of exact 1/60 s steps (27.83, 31.36), so the real frame steps were longer than 1/60 s: a running game's phase is ahead of the ideal 60 Hz count by the summed overruns, and it differs between runs. A viewer can only reproduce a given phase exactly, not predict the live one.

notes: The glide of the finger cursor is not on this clock: GUICursorHand_StepToward moves a fixed fraction per UI frame.
open_questions: ? The frame timer's maximum step and the value of g_GUICore+2104.

name: UnitColoursAreATintThenAFade
summary: A battle unit's 16 colours are its palette row put through one tint rule (status tints, ambient light), then moved by the palette manager's timed fades; the result is uploaded to the emulated video memory, where the HD layer reads it back to build the unit's textures.

behavior.text: the row is one of the 16 rows of 16 colours of the classic sprite file, kept in the unit's look pool record (sub_14026E838 copies them and applies the CharShape colour override); the scene unit's byte +11 picks the row.

SceneUnit_ApplyStatusTint picks the tint: one of eight status tints by the unit's flag dword, else SceneUnit_RunPlacement gives the plain row with ambient offsets (0, -4, -8 or -12 on all channels by its argument, adjusted by scene variables 35 and 36).
the tint rule (UnitClut_TintRow) has four modes (plain, halved, grey, half grey) plus an offset per channel; the result is the unit slot's base row in bank 3.
timed fades (ClutFade_SetTarget, ClutManager_Update) move the shown colours from where they are to a target computed from the base row, in 8 or 32 table steps, optionally back and forth.

the unit under the cursor at deployment pulses by such a fade: target = base row + 8 on all channels, 8 steps each way. The brightest colour of the test row (red 26, green 25, blue 23) moved by (0,0,1) (1,1,2) (1,2,3) (2,3,4) (3,3,5) (3,4,6) (4,5,7) on the seven steps, as the 8-step table gives for the distances 5, 6 and 8.

ClutManager_Upload copies the final image into the emulated video memory; HdLayer_BuildTextures reads a draw record's 16 colours from there by the record's palette id, hashes them and keeps one texture per piece and hash.
so every colour effect on a unit in battle is a change of its 16 colours before the texture pass; nothing after the pass knows the palette.

notes: The menu side has no manager: CharaRender_BuildAtlasTexture loads the classic file's rows itself (CharaPalette_LoadClassic) and applies the same tint rule inline by its flag bits.
open_questions: ? which status each tint flag stands for; ? other producers of unit colours (the fade callers sub_1401EAAF8.. were not read).

name: UnitFaceFromSpriteNumber
summary: The small unit face is chosen from the sprite number through three portrait-code tables, then a face number, and the face number is capped at 0xCD; the status card's large job picture follows a different path through the job type.

behavior.text: the face cap is a compare with 0xCD at 0x1402C0816 (Unit_GetSpriteSetId) and 0x1401F3A03 (sub_1401F3858); the two other cap sites (0x214272 in sub_140214134, 0x21519D in TurnPanel_SetUnitPanel, 0x215786 in TurnPanel_SetTag) compare against a register.

the chain is sprite number, portrait code (the word tables of SpriteTablesEndAtSprite169; the table used depends on the screen: 0x683A70 menus, 0x680070 battle, 0x6807C0 the party list), face number (code up to 0x9F through the dword table at 0x7146D0; 0xB0 to 0xC7 special cases; else -1 and the callers keep the code, capped), a few remaps in FaceNumber_Remap, then the texture name wldface_<number>_<colour> with colour = ((code >> 10) & 3) + 8 (the format string is a row of the UI texture path table).
a sprite whose portrait code is 0 shows face 1 (the main character's); portrait numbers 170 to 204 are taken.

portrait codes of 0x53 and above mean story characters: the battle reader sub_140300D74 then reads a byte at +0x2F of a global character record (the load at 0x140301451), so a code of 212 there crashed in battle.

SpriteId_ToShape is the function that turns a code up to 0x9F into the face number through g_SpriteIdToShape and answers fixed values for the codes 176, 183, 188 to 201, 205; its current name describes the scene sprite use, the face-number use above is the same function reached from the portrait readers (I).

open_questions: ? whether the name SpriteId_ToShape should become a face-number name; both uses read the same table and need a sheet note.

name: UnitFaceIndexReadsTheTableAfterTheHdTable
summary: Unit_GetFaceIndex reads the face index of a monster job from the table right after the HD sheet entry table, through a virtual base that falls inside the HD table, so an address-range census counts it as an HD reader by mistake.

behavior.text: for a job word at +0x24 between 94 and 141 the function returns dword_140715378[job]; 0x140715378 is 392 bytes into the HD table, and the lowest address read (job 94) is 0x1407154F0, past the HD table's 680 bytes.
0x1407154F0 holds 48 dwords, 62 to 77, three jobs per monster family (g_MonsterFaceIndexByJob).

name: UnitMovementAnimationTables
summary: Eight data tables, one per sprite class, hold the unit's movement animations only (standing, walking, floating, turning, jumping, a few single-frame poses): a row per step, keyed by animation id and step number; attack and spell animations are not in them.

behavior.text: CharaAnim_ReadStep takes the class from the sprite attribute table (byte 1 of the 4-byte row of the shape), picks that class's table, and finds the row by key = animation id and key2 = step number; the row gives an opcode (dword), an operand (byte) and a delay (byte, in ticks of 1/60 s).

the class equals the shape's sequence kind: the humanoid layout with robes and casters uses class 1, the martial humanoid layout class 0, and the other layouts classes 2 to 7 (one class per sequence kind of the sprite attribute table).

opcode 1 shows the SHP frame whose number is the operand for the delay; opcode 144 restarts the animation; opcode 118 shifts the unit's x offset by a signed amount; opcodes 149, 150, 153 and 154 are small offset steps; 148, 152 and 102 appear in some classes; opcode 0 is an empty step. Only 1, 118, 144 and the 149 range are decoded in the code (CharaAnim_Step); the others are read from the rows only.

each class holds 21 to 25 animation ids out of the range 1 to 73. Ids 1 to 5 are one-step poses showing frames 3, 2, 1, 8 and 7 of the martial layout (the eight standing views); ids 6 to 11 are loops over five body frames in a ping-pong order with three delay sets; ids 20 and 21 hold a single frame with offset steps; ids 24 and 25 are loops like 6 and 7 with a shifted start; ids 42 and 43 step through the eight standing views in turn; ids 56 and 57 are 19-step sequences with offset opcodes that end on a held frame; ids 52, 53, 62, 63, 72 and 73 are one-step poses showing frames 23, 24, 31, 33, 72 and 73 (robed layout: 72 and 73 show 64 and 65).

from what the steps draw, ids 6 to 11 look like a walk cycle (three speeds, front and back), ids 42 and 43 a turn on the spot through the eight views, and ids 56 and 57 a jump (a rise, a held frame, a landing); the game itself carries no names for these animations and the other ids are not given a reading here.

a loop of ids 6 to 11 is 8 show-frame steps followed by a restart row; in the two humanoid classes the frames are five body frames per facing in a ping-pong order; the three speeds differ only in the delays.

class 0 (martial humanoid layout) and class 1 (robed and caster layout) show the same frame numbers for ids 1 to 11, 20, 21, 24, 25, 56 and 57, differ on animations 72 and 73 (different frame numbers), and class 1 has no rows for ids 42 and 43 (turn on the spot).
the attack, cast and hurt animations are not here; the classic animation file carries them (see BattleMotionNumbers); the menu and job-tree renderer reads only these tables.

notes: Table ids: the eight tables are loaded by ids 108, 112, 113, 114, 248, 115, 116 and 117 in class order. Fields of the rows: the table columns Unknown8 (opcode) and UnknownC (operand in the low byte, delay in the second byte) are now identified.
open_questions: ? the meaning of opcodes 148, 150, 152, 153, 154 and 102 beyond 'small offset or flag step'; ? whether class 2 (the chocobo layout) is used by anything but its one sprite; ? which code reads the battle unit's animation number and turns it into the classic animation pointer (see BattleMotionNumbers).

name: UnlockMaskStreamRunsIntoLearnedBitsPastIndex23
summary: The unit's unlock mask is 3 bytes (24 bits) read through a bit stream, and the learned-ability bits follow it directly in the same record, so a bit read at a job index of 24 or more lands in the learned bits of the first jobs.

behavior.text: record layout: unlock mask at A+47, B+120, C+159 (3 bytes) followed by the learned bits at A+50, B+123, C+162 (3 bytes per job index); the bit reader pointer is set from these (qword_143C49BF0 stores in JobList_BuildForPartyUnit, sub_14028668C, JobAbilityList_Build, sub_14028A474, JobScreen_BuildLearnableList, sub_14031E50C, Unit_BuildJobUnlockMask, Party_CountMasteredJobs).

JobList_Build reads mask bits 0..21 only; Job_IsLockedForParty skips Job_IdToIndex(job) bits and reads one bit of each party member's mask, and Job_IdToIndex answers 0 for every job outside 74..93 and 160..161, so any other job id reads bit 0 there.

Unit_BuildJobUnlockMask builds only bits for job index 1..19 from the 12-byte rows of g_JobNeedLevelRows (nibble per job index, 24 indices) and clears bit 0x8 by the mastery check of two jobs; it has no row for a job index above 23.

JobList_RecomputeAvailability and GameState_ResetJobFlags work on g_UnitJobFlags: 21 new-job flags at offset 0 (jobs 74..93, 160, 161 by index) and 125 job-type disable flags at offset 21 (key = the job row's type word, below 125); a job index above 20 used as an index into the first part would address the disable flags.

name: UnormStoreRoundsHalfDown
scope: GPU (the test machine's GPU and driver)
summary: When a shader stores a float into an 8-bit UNORM target, an exact half rounds down: 16.5 stores 16, 9.5 stores 9.

behavior.text: 787 values of the name tag's shadow draw sit exactly on a half; all of them store the lower value, and with this rule every changed value of the four shadow draws is reproduced. D3D allows implementations to differ here, so other GPUs may round these values up.

behavior.basis: (second capture, the ring glow's bilinear upscale)
behavior.text: rounding halves down gives 0 differences of 27744 values; rounding them up gives 1384.

name: UsableAbilityListLearnedBitGroup
summary: The usable-ability list reads a unit's learned bits per job group. For a skillset outside 5..0x17 that is the unit's primary or secondary skillset it takes group 0, which is right for the special characters' own sets.

behavior.text: sub_14030E368 picks the group as skillset - 5 for 5..0x17, the hidden Dark Knight job's for 0xE0, 0 for a set equal to the unit's +0x12 or +0x192, and all 24 bits for any other set; every path meets at 0x14030E55A.
an Archer whose primary skillset was a set outside 5..0x17 listed its slots 1 and 2 as learned from group 0 (the unit's Squire bits 0x60) and not the ability learned in its Archer group.

name: VertexColourBytesTruncated
summary: A UI node's vertex colour reaches the shader as bytes: each channel is the product of the node colour and its opacity, truncated to an integer. An opacity of 0.19999998807907104 on alpha 255 gives 50, not 51.

behavior.text: the floor's stone image (opacity 0.19999998807907104) fits a weight of 0.981 x 0.2 = 50 / 255 (least squares over 389043 pixels); with alpha 50 / 255 the floor model is 97.9 % exact, with 51 / 255 or the float 47.9 %.
the node colour path combines bytes with integer truncation (sheet GUINode_ApplyAnimChannels: colour c = sampled * node byte / 255, truncating).

name: WidgetRootsAreLayers
scope: every UI widget (the Job Tree, the finger cursor, the footer guides)
summary: Every widget's root component is drawn into its own layer record, whether or not it has an effect: the renderer's feature byte at r+606621 is 1 from the initialiser and the widget byte at +83 is 1 for all 51 widgets of the running game, so ComponentLayer_Begin opens a layer at the root. Components with an enabled effect group or a non-zero blend type open further layers inside it. UIB nodes of kind Layer (names like Layer00, LayerRoot, LayerBranches) never open a layer.

behavior.text: ComponentLayer_Begin: the layer is forced when r+606621 is set and (widget +83 is set and the context depth +552 is 0 (the root), or the component byte +561 is set); it is opened when the context carries no layer (+553, which nothing in the code writes: always 0) and either the effects collector reports one or the force applies.
widget +83 = 1 in all 51 entries of the widget vector at g_GUICore + 24; the cursor widget (ffto_common_cursor) and the Job Tree widgets are among them.

the finger cursor's Widget component has blend 0 and no effect enabled, so its layer comes only from the widget-root rule: the glove is drawn into a layer target and the layer is then blended onto the frame, which is the two 8-bit stores the captures show.

the other components of the Job Tree that open a layer on their own are those with an effect group enabled in the property block: UnitSelect (glow), the Line components (glow, radius and strength from state tracks), TextBoardJobName (drop shadow) and Cross (single float group).
component byte +561 is set by addon code of the battle UI (seven small functions), not by anything Job Tree specific.

open_questions: ? who sets widget +83 (read as a dword field; no direct byte writer found).

name: WorldMapLocationsAndBattleEntry
scope: world map free roam, Locations list, travel to a battleground, battle deployment
summary: How a battle is entered from the world map, and which screens and memory fields show it, as seen live.

behavior.text: the free-roam world map has no focused widget (focus empty, glove at the screen centre) and shows the footer 'Main Menu | Locations | Zoom Out | Move Cursor | Center on Ramza' plus the current objective text on worldmap_top_layer.uib ('Head to Dorter and find information on the Corpse Brigade's movements.'). A does nothing there unless the cursor is on a settlement.

X opens the Locations list (worldmap_base_info.uib): tabs Settlements (Merchant City of Dorter, Magick City of Gariland, Eagrose Castle), Battlegrounds (The Siedge Weald, Mandalia Plain) and Miscellaneous; RB switches the tab. A on an entry closes the list and puts the map cursor on that location (focus worldmap_map_all.uib shows its name); a second A starts the walk there with no focus and no text.

arriving at The Siedge Weald loaded the battle deployment screen (ffto_battle_sortie_ver02.uib, visible only then): footer 'Zoom | Select Tile | Previous Unit | Commence Battle', text 'Remaining: 3', 'Battle Members', 'Press [] to place a unit on this tile'. START opens 'Commence battle? Yes / No' (glove at about 959,923); A on Yes starts the battle.

after Yes, while enemy and guest units took their turns, the memory state read as if nothing had started: focus still ffto_battle_sortie_ver02.uib, scene kind 'in-engine cutscene, event 31' with skip allowed 0, turn slot 0xFFFFFFFF, no text drawn; pad A / B / X / START, Esc, Enter, Space and hold Y / hold Space changed nothing, and window screenshots showed the battle running (a unit's movement range in red, a different unit each frame). When Ramza's turn came the fields caught up (focus ffto_battle_command.uib, turn slot 16, player_turn, menu row 0, the command menu drawn) with event 31 and the sortie screen still listed. The sortie screen stays loaded for the whole battle.

the footer (ffto_footer_02.uib) tells the two phases apart: 'Zoom | Select Tile | Previous Unit | Commence Battle' on the deployment screen; during the enemy and guest turns it reads 'Pause Battle', 'Next', 'Status', 'View Battlefield', 'Center on Ramza', 'Change Combat Set' (the first label alternates between 'Pause Battle' and 'Change Display' every few seconds). The 'Next' in that footer is a permanent hint, not a message page.
Esc opens ffto_pause.uib during this phase ('Esc resumes, hold Space skips the cutscene'); closing it brings up a ffto_battle_dialog.uib screen and a notice-dialog agent with no text drawn.

notes: Window capture: the debugger's `shot` command (window capture that works while the game is in the background).
